items.title: 11.5 Maximum and Minimum Values of Given Functions of the Type a + b sin theta, a + b cos theta, a + b sin(c theta + d), a + b cos(c theta + d) and reciprocals

source_refs.note: Book p. 211-213: 11.5 heading with its five types, sinusoidal functions, vertical shift, amplitude, period, phase shift, graph of 1 + 3 sin 2 theta, M = a + |b|, m = a - |b|, Note on amplitude, Example 2

blocks.text: The printed heading lists the types of functions studied in this section:

items: The reciprocal of the above, where \(a\), \(b\), \(c\) and \(d\) are real numbers.

blocks.text: The trigonometric functions like sine and cosine are periodic functions, because their values repeat over regular intervals. These functions are fundamental in mathematics because their values repeat in definite cycles, and they are used to model many real-life situations, such as radio waves, light waves and alternating current in electricity. They are also known as a specific case of sinusoidal functions.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Before this section, recall two facts from the graphs of sine and cosine:
1. \(-1 \le \sin\theta \le 1\) and \(-1 \le \cos\theta \le 1\) for every \(\theta\).
2. \(\sin\theta\) and \(\cos\theta\) repeat after \(2\pi\).
Everything in this section is built on these two facts. "Sinusoidal" simply means "shaped like the sine wave".

The functions of the form
\[f(\theta) = a + b\sin\theta\]
\[g(\theta) = a + b\cos\theta\]
\[f_{1}(\theta) = a + b\sin(c\theta + d)\]
\[g_{1}(\theta) = a + b\cos(c\theta + d)\]
are the most common types of sinusoidal functions.

Now consider the general form of a sinusoidal function
\[f_{1}(\theta) = a + b\sin(c\theta + d) \quad \text{...(i)}\]

items: Vertical shift \(a\): the vertical translation of the graph of a periodic function, obtained by shifting the entire graph upward or downward. This shift, also known as the vertical displacement, moves the function's position along the \(y\)-axis without changing its shape or period. The line \(y = a\) is the midline of the wave.
Amplitude \(b\): the maximum height of the wave measured from its midline (its size is \(|b|\)).
Period: the period of (i) is equal to \(\frac{2\pi}{c}\).

Phase shift \(d\): it indicates the horizontal translation of the graph, i.e. how far the wave is shifted left or right along the \(x\)-axis. A positive \(d\) shifts the graph to the left, while a negative \(d\) shifts it to the right, changing the starting point of the wave without changing its shape or period.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why is the period \(\frac{2\pi}{c}\)? The sine repeats when its angle grows by \(2\pi\). The angle here is \(c\theta + d\); it grows by \(2\pi\) when \(\theta\) grows by \(\frac{2\pi}{c}\) (taking \(c > 0\); in general the period is \(\frac{2\pi}{|c|}\)).
About the phase shift: \(c\theta + d = c\left(\theta + \frac{d}{c}\right)\), so the graph actually moves through a distance \(\frac{d}{c}\) (left when it is positive). When \(c = 1\) this distance is exactly \(d\).
None of \(c\) and \(d\) changes the maximum or minimum value: they only stretch or slide the wave sideways.

For example, consider the function \(f(\theta) = 1 + 3\sin(2\theta)\). Here \(a = 1\) is the vertical shift, the amplitude is \(|b| = |3| = 3\), and the period is \(\frac{2\pi}{2} = \pi\), as shown in the figure.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: On the book's graph the label of the tick between \(\frac{3\pi}{2}\) and \(2\pi\) is printed as \(\frac{3\pi}{4}\). That tick is \(\frac{7\pi}{4}\), where the second minimum \(-2\) occurs. Our figure is plotted exactly from \(f(\theta) = 1 + 3\sin 2\theta\).

Now, finding the maximum and minimum values of the functions \(f(\theta) = a + b\sin(c\theta + d)\) and \(g(\theta) = a + b\cos(c\theta + d)\) is not a difficult task. We know that the maximum absolute values of sine and cosine are equal to 1, so the maximum value of the product \(b\sin\theta\) is \(|b|\).

Thus the maximum value of \(f(\theta)\) is \(M = a + |b|\), whenever \(\sin\theta = 1\) or \(\cos\theta = 1\), where \(M\) denotes the maximum value of the function.
The minimum value of a function is \(m = a - |b|\), whenever \(\sin\theta = -1\) or \(\cos\theta = -1\), and \(m\) denotes the minimum value of the function.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The values \(M = a + |b|\) and \(m = a - |b|\) are correct, but the conditions printed with them hold only when \(b > 0\). When \(b < 0\) they swap: the maximum \(a + |b|\) occurs where the sine (or cosine) equals \(-1\), and the minimum \(a - |b|\) where it equals \(1\). For example \(5 - 2\cos 3x\) is largest when \(\cos 3x = -1\) (see Example 2(ii)).

blocks.text_alt: Maximum value M equals a plus the absolute value of b
Minimum value m equals a minus the absolute value of b

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why these formulas work: since \(-1 \le \sin\theta \le 1\), multiplying by \(|b|\) gives \(-|b| \le b\sin\theta \le |b|\) (the sign of \(b\) only decides which end is reached when). Adding \(a\) to every part:
\[a - |b| \le a + b\sin\theta \le a + |b|\]
Both ends are actually reached, because the sine really does take the values \(1\) and \(-1\). The same holds for cosine and for \(\sin(c\theta + d)\), \(\cos(c\theta + d)\): the angle changes, but the values still run over the whole interval from \(-1\) to \(1\).

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text:
The absolute value of \(b\) is called the amplitude of \(f(\theta) = a + b\sin\theta\). The value of the amplitude can also be found using the formula
\[\text{Amplitude} = \dfrac{\text{Maximum value} - \text{Minimum value}}{2}\]

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Check the Note with the formulas: \(\dfrac{M - m}{2} = \dfrac{(a + |b|) - (a - |b|)}{2} = \dfrac{2|b|}{2} = |b|\). In the same way the midline is the average: \(\dfrac{M + m}{2} = a\). These two facts let you build a model from a maximum and a minimum (used in 11.5.1).

blocks.title: Example 2
blocks.problem:
Find the maximum and minimum values of the following functions:
(i) \(2 + 3\sin x\)  (ii) \(5 - 2\cos 3x\)  (iii) reciprocal of (ii)
steps:
Given: (i) \(2 + 3\sin x\), (ii) \(5 - 2\cos 3x\), (iii) \(\dfrac{1}{5 - 2\cos 3x}\).
To find: the maximum value \(M\) and the minimum value \(m\) of each.
Method: (i) and (ii) have the form \(a + b\sin(\ldots)\) or \(a + b\cos(\ldots)\), so \(M = a + |b|\) and \(m = a - |b|\). For (iii) we use the rule for reciprocals of positive quantities: the larger the denominator, the smaller the fraction.

Step 1: (i) identify \(a\) and \(b\)
Let \(f(x) = 2 + 3\sin x\).
\[a = 2,\quad b = 3\]
Why: comparing with \(a + b\sin x\). Since \(b > 0\), the maximum occurs when \(\sin x = 1\) and the minimum when \(\sin x = -1\).

Step 2: (i) maximum and minimum
\[M = a + |b| = 2 + 3 = 5\]
\[m = a - |b| = 2 - 3 = -1\]
Why: \(\sin x\) runs from \(-1\) to \(1\), so \(3\sin x\) runs from \(-3\) to \(3\), and adding 2 gives \(-1\) to \(5\).
Check: \(\sin x = 1\) gives \(2 + 3 = 5\); \(\sin x = -1\) gives \(2 - 3 = -1\).

Step 3: (ii) identify \(a\) and \(b\)
Let \(f(x) = 5 - 2\cos 3x\).
\[a = 5,\quad b = -2\]
The book prints: "The maximum value of f(x) will occur when \(\cos 3x = 1\)".
Working it out: here \(b\) is negative, so \(-2\cos 3x\) is largest when \(\cos 3x\) is smallest, i.e. when \(\cos 3x = -1\); the minimum occurs when \(\cos 3x = 1\).
Why: multiplying by a negative number reverses the order: the smallest \(\cos 3x\) gives the largest \(-2\cos 3x\).

Step 4: (ii) maximum and minimum
\[M = a + |b| = 5 + |-2|\]
\[= 5 + 2 = 7\]
\[m = a - |b| = 5 - |-2|\]
\[= 5 - 2 = 3\]
Why: the formulas use \(|b| = 2\), so the sign of \(b\) does not change the values, only where they occur. The \(3x\) inside changes the period, not the range.
Check: \(\cos 3x = -1\): \(5 - 2(-1) = 7\); \(\cos 3x = 1\): \(5 - 2(1) = 3\).

Step 5: (iii) write the reciprocal
\[g(x) = \dfrac{1}{5 - 2\cos 3x}\]
First find the maximum and minimum of \(5 - 2\cos 3x\): they are 7 and 3 (part (ii)).
Why: \(g\) is built from part (ii), so its values depend directly on the values of \(5 - 2\cos 3x\).

Step 6: (iii) take reciprocals
\[\text{Max of } g(x) = \dfrac{1}{m} = \dfrac{1}{3} \approx 0.33\]
\[\text{Min of } g(x) = \dfrac{1}{M} = \dfrac{1}{7} \approx 0.14\]
Why: the denominator always lies between 3 and 7, so it is positive. For positive numbers, the reciprocal of the smallest is the largest and the reciprocal of the largest is the smallest.
Check: \(\dfrac{1}{3} > \dfrac{1}{7}\), and both values are reached (at \(\cos 3x = 1\) and \(\cos 3x = -1\)).
blocks.answer:
(i) Maximum 5, minimum \(-1\).
(ii) Maximum 7 (when \(\cos 3x = -1\)), minimum 3 (when \(\cos 3x = 1\)).
(iii) Maximum \(\frac{1}{3} \approx 0.33\), minimum \(\frac{1}{7} \approx 0.14\).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: In Example 2(ii) the book prints that the maximum occurs when \(\cos 3x = 1\) and the minimum when \(\cos 3x = -1\). Since \(b = -2\) is negative, it is the other way round: the maximum 7 occurs when \(\cos 3x = -1\) and the minimum 3 when \(\cos 3x = 1\). The values 7 and 3 printed in the book are correct.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text: For a reciprocal, do not simply copy the maximum and minimum: they swap places. Also, the rule "reciprocal of the maximum is the minimum" only works when the expression never becomes zero or negative; here \(5 - 2\cos 3x \ge 3 > 0\), so it is safe.

blocks.title: Exam tip
blocks.text: For any question of this section write three things first: \(a\), \(b\) and \(|b|\). Then \(M = a + |b|\), \(m = a - |b|\). The numbers \(c\) and \(d\) inside the bracket never change \(M\) and \(m\); they only change the period and the position of the wave.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. For \(a + b\sin(c\theta + d)\) and \(a + b\cos(c\theta + d)\): vertical shift (midline) \(a\), amplitude \(|b|\), period \(\frac{2\pi}{c}\), phase shift from \(d\).
2. \(M = a + |b|\) and \(m = a - |b|\).
3. If \(b > 0\) the maximum is where the sine/cosine is \(1\); if \(b < 0\) it is where the sine/cosine is \(-1\).
4. Amplitude \(= \frac{M - m}{2}\) and midline \(a = \frac{M + m}{2}\).
5. For a positive reciprocal \(\frac{1}{a + b\sin(\ldots)}\): maximum \(= \frac{1}{m}\), minimum \(= \frac{1}{M}\).

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Writing \(M = a + b\) with a negative \(b\): for \(5 - 2\cos 3x\) this gives \(3\), which is the minimum. Always use \(|b|\).
2. Thinking that \(c\) changes the maximum: \(\sin 3x\) and \(\sin x\) both run from \(-1\) to \(1\).
3. Forgetting to swap the maximum and minimum when taking the reciprocal.
4. Confusing the amplitude with the whole height of the wave: the amplitude is half of \(M - m\).
